questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Level Surface
questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=9{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-z,$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=0.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ 9{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-z & =0 \\ z & =9{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ z & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{1/9}+{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=0$ is the elliptic paraboloid $z=\frac{{x}^{2}}{1/9}+{y}^{2}.$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+z-2,$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-2.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=-2.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+z-2 & =-2 \\ z & ={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=-2$ is the hyperbolic paraboloid $z={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Describing a Level Surface of a Function
questions.problem: Which of the following describes the level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2y+z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2y+z) & =c \\ x-2y+z & ={e}^{c}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the exponent ${e}^{c}$ is positive for all $-\infty <c<\infty .$ If we let ${e}^{c}={r}^{2},$ we get a family of planes:

$$
x-2y+z={r}^{2},\,r\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following describes the level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)=-{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+z+3?$
questions.worked_solution:
The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ -{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+z+3 & =c \\ z & ={x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}+c-3\end{aligned}
$$

If we let $c-3=C,$ we get a family of elliptic paraboloids:

$$
z={x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}+C,\,C\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following describes the $c$-level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}},$ where $c>0?$
questions.worked_solution:
The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}} & =c \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & ={c}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get a family of hyperboloids of one sheet:

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{c}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{c}^{2}}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{{c}^{2}}=1,\,c\in (0,\infty ).
$$

A family of hyperboloids of one sheet: $\frac{{x}^{2}}{{c}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{c}^{2}}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{{c}^{2}}=1$

questions.problem: Which of the following describes the level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡z?$
questions.worked_solution:
The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡z & =c \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡z & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-c \\ z & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-c}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get a family of curves:

$$
z={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-c},\,c\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Level Surface of a Function Passing Through a Point
questions.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{x-y+z-1}$ that passes through the point $P(1,1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,1) & ={e}^{1-1+1-1} \\  & ={e}^{0} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=1.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {e}^{x-y+z-1} & =1 \\ x-y+z-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(1,1,1)$ is the plane $x-y+z-1=0.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Level Surface of a Function Passing Through a Point
questions.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{{z}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}}$ that passes through the point $P(3,1,6).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3,1,6) & =\frac{{6}^{2}}{{3}^{2}+9({1}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{36}{18} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=2.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{{z}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}} & =2 \\ {z}^{2} & =2({x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}) \\ {z}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}+18{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(3,1,6)$ is the elliptic cone
 ${z}^{2}=2{x}^{2}+18{y}^{2}.$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2y+3z)$ that passes through the point $P(1,1,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P$:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,0) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+2(1)+3(0))=\operatorname{ln}⁡3\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=\operatorname{ln}⁡3.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2y+3z) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ x+2y+3z & =3 \\ x+2y+3z-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(1,1,0)$ is the plane $x+2y+3z-3=0.$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+3(y-1)^{2}-{z}^{2}$ that passes through the point $P(4,2,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P$:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4,2,1) & ={4}^{2}+3(2-1)^{2}-{1}^{2}=18\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=18.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {x}^{2}+3(y-1)^{2}-{z}^{2} & =18 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{18}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{6}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{18} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(4,2,1)$ is the hyperboloid of one sheet $\frac{{x}^{2}}{18}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{6}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{18}=1.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Level Surface
canonical_examples.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z) = x^2+4y^2-z,$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z) = c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c = 0.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-z & =0 \\ z & ={x}^{2}+4{y}^{2} \\ z & ={x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{1/4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=0$ is the elliptic paraboloid $z = x^2+\dfrac{y^2}{{1/4}}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Describing a Level Surface of a Function
canonical_examples.problem: Find the family of surfaces that describe the level surfaces of the function $f(x,y, z) = \ln(x^2 + 2y^2 - z^2).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}) & =c \\ {x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & ={e}^{c} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{e}^{c}}+\frac{2{y}^{2}}{{e}^{c}}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{{e}^{c}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get a family of hyperboloids of one sheet:

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{e^c} + \dfrac{y^2}{e^c/2} - \dfrac{z^2}{e^c} =  1, \qquad c \in (-\infty,\infty)
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Level Surface of a Function Passing Through a Point
canonical_examples.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z) = \sin{xyz}$ that passes through the point $P\left(\pi,1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
  f\left(\pi,1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&= \sin \left(\pi\cdot 1 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sin{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)} = 1}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z) = c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c = 1.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡xyz & =1 \\ xyz & =\frac{\pi }{2}+2\pi k\end{aligned}
$$

where $k$ is any integer.

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P\left(\pi,1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ is the surface $xyz= \dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2\pi k,$ where $k$ is any integer.
